source.title: BabyVLM-V2: Toward Developmentally Grounded Pretraining and Benchmarking of Vision Foundation Models
source.authors: Shengao Wang; Wen-Qi Wang; Ze-Cheng Wang; M. Whitton; Michael Wakeham; Arjun Chandra; J. Huang; Pengyue Zhu; He Chen; David Li; Jeffrey Li; Shawn Li; Andrew Zagula; Amy Zhao; Andrew Zhu; Sayaka Nakamura; Y. Yamamoto; Jerry Jun Yokono; Aaron Mueller; Bryan A. Plummer; Kate Saenko; V. Saligrama; Bo-Qing Gong

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream-task results across instruction-data fractions and an explicit model-size comparison. These are different from the original held-out language-model loss measurements and compute-allocation fits.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws as context and describes instruction-data-fraction results as a qualitative scaling-like trend. It does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The size-doubling comparison and instruction-data-fraction results bear on downstream performance with scale; cited scaling-law results are not extracted.
record.test_reason: This is a benchmark and framework paper for small vision-language models trained on infant headcam data. It cites scaling laws as context and calls one fine-tuning result 'a clear scaling-like trend.' It reports no held-out loss, no power-law fit, no extrapolation and no compute allocation. Its two scale-related observations do not test any version. The first varies instruction-tuning data fraction for one VLM and shows the result only in a figure, with no fitted form. The second is a one-sentence remark, without numbers, that doubling the language-model size gave no significant gain. That remark justifies a design choice in a heavily data-limited regime and is not a scaling measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but misplaced in emphasis. The authors' main conclusion is that BabyVLM-V2 gives a developmentally grounded pretraining set, a compact from-scratch VLM and a validated DevCV Toolbox benchmark. They report that the compact model is competitive with similar-size open models and beats GPT-4o on some math tasks. The scaling-like instruction-data trend and the no-gain-from-doubling remark are appendix side observations.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream vision-language benchmark accuracy, not held-out language-model loss; it varies instruction data and compares one doubled language-backbone size rather than fitting scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance changes with instruction-data fraction; the pretrained model outperforms the non-pretrained variant across the tested fractions.

fits_no_version.finding: DevCV Toolbox overall accuracy rises with the fraction of instruction-tuning data, for both pretrained and non-pretrained baby models. The pretrained model stays ahead, especially at small fractions. Values are figure-only (Fig. 17) and the authors call the trend qualitative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-data quantity improves downstream accuracy in small from-scratch VLMs, with pretraining improving sample efficiency.

fits_no_version.finding: Doubling the language-backbone size (from about 1.1B) of a VLM trained on about 1M infant-headcam samples gave 'no significant gain,' with no numbers given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In severely data-limited from-scratch VLM training, larger language backbones may not improve downstream accuracy.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says the dataset, checkpoints, scripts, and evaluation samples will be released in the future.
record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (as stated in the supplied study metadata)
record.problems: The instruction-data-fraction results are reported qualitatively in a figure without numerical values in the text. The doubled-size result has no task-level numbers or stated uncertainty, and only one size comparison is described.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Fine-tuning data and model size are varied, but no power-law form is fitted or checked.
No systematic relation of downstream accuracy to model scale or pretraining loss; only one unquantified size comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tests/T2 classification and V6 labels overstate the study. Neither scale observation is a scaling measurement: one is a qualitative, figure-only fine-tuning sweep and the other is an unquantified design-justification remark. Scaling laws appear only as cited context (refs 17, 22, 23).

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No power-law fit or extrapolation from smaller runs is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trend is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study trains a vision-language model and varies instruction-data fraction, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in vision or fine-tuning.

Tests are limited to downstream benchmark accuracy under instruction-data-fraction variation and one language-backbone size comparison; there is no measured relationship to pretraining loss or a broad predictive scaling curve.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending is reported.

rows.value: Figure only; text states the pretrained model consistently outperforms the non-pretrained variant across all data fractions and that performance improves as the fraction increases.

rows.check: This row measures downstream accuracy against instruction-tuning data fraction for a single VLM, with figure-only values and no functional form. V6 concerns how downstream performance tracks model or pretraining scale or loss. V5 needs the power-law form, which the study never fits. The qualitative increase is moved to fits_no_version.

reader_labels.reason: The text reports improving downstream performance as instruction-data fraction increases for both variants; the pretrained model also consistently exceeds the non-pretrained one (r1–r2). The trend is described qualitatively, with values shown only in the figure.
